sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers (called edges or PoPs) that caches content close to end users, so requests for static assets, video chunks, or even dynamic API responses are served from a nearby edge rather than a distant origin — reducing latency, offloading origin traffic, and absorbing traffic spikes.
A CDN solves the fundamental problem that the speed of light is slow and the internet is a tree. If your origin is in Virginia and your user is in Mumbai, every byte has to traverse ~12,000 km of fiber, which at two-thirds the speed of light in fiber is at least 60 ms one-way — meaning a 240 ms round trip just for the TCP handshake, plus another 240 ms for TLS, plus the actual request and response. Caching content at an edge PoP in Mumbai collapses that to a few milliseconds. CDNs like Akamai, Cloudflare, Fastly, AWS CloudFront, and Edgecast run global networks of hundreds to thousands of PoPs, and use DNS-based geographic routing to send each user to the nearest one. Akamai alone is estimated to deliver 15–30% of all internet traffic. The economic case is even stronger: origin bandwidth is expensive (cloud egress fees are $0.05–0.09/GB), while CDN bandwidth is 2–5x cheaper per GB and offloads origin CPU and TLS handshake cost.

CDNs split into two caching models. **Origin pull** (the default for web CDNs like Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront) means the edge fetches content from the origin on first request, caches it, and serves subsequent requests from cache until the TTL expires or the cache is invalidated. This is "lazy population" — only content that users actually request gets cached. **Origin push** (used by Netflix Open Connect and some video CDNs) means the origin proactively uploads content to edges in advance of demand — Netflix pre-positions new episode encodes onto Open Connect appliances inside ISPs' datacenters hours before release so that when 10 million people hit "play" at the same moment, the bytes are already local. Origin push is essential for massive concurrent demand like a Netflix premiere; origin pull would melt the origin under the thundering herd. The trade-off is that origin push requires the CDN to predict demand, while origin pull adapts automatically but cannot scale a single viral URL.

The cache key is the critical concept. The default cache key is `{URL path} + {query string}`, but production CDNs let you customize it. Cloudflare's "Cache Key" lets you ignore certain query parameters (e.g., `?utm_source=` tracking params), include or exclude headers, and normalize the case. Vary headers (e.g., `Vary: Accept-Encoding`) tell the cache to store separate entries for gzip vs brotli vs identity. Getting the cache key wrong is the #1 cause of CDN incidents: a key that includes a per-user session cookie will defeat caching entirely, while a key that ignores a meaningful header (e.g., `Accept-Language`) will serve the wrong language to half your users. Modern CDNs also support surrogate keys (Fastly's `Surrogate-Key` header, Cloudflare's `Cache-Tag`) which let you purge all assets for a particular product or article in one call, rather than purging individual URLs.

Cache invalidation is the hard problem. The naive model is TTL-based: a cached asset expires after N seconds and the next request re-fetches from origin. This is fine for static assets but causes "stale window" problems where users see outdated content for up to TTL seconds after a publish. Real-time invalidation is the alternative: when you publish a new article, you call the CDN's purge API (`POST /purge` with the URL or surrogate key) and the CDN evicts that entry across all edges within seconds. Cloudflare's purge API propagates in ~30 seconds globally; Fastly's in ~150 ms because it uses instant purge over its global messaging fabric. The trade-off: instant purge is operationally expensive (the CDN has to track every cached object by key) and risks a thundering herd if you purge a hot URL — the next request hits origin while thousands of concurrent requests wait. The standard mitigation is "stale-while-revalidate" (`Cache-Control: max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=60`) — the CDN serves the stale entry for up to 60 seconds while asynchronously refreshing from origin, so users never see latency spikes and origin never sees a thundering herd.

Edge compute is the next evolution. Instead of just caching, modern CDNs run your code at the edge: Cloudflare Workers (V8 isolates, 300+ PoPs), AWS Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions (run on every CloudFront edge), Fastly Compute@Edge (Wasm). Netflix uses edge compute for A/B routing at the edge (which variant of the homepage does this user see?), for personalization headers (inject user-region into the request before it hits origin), and for bot mitigation (challenge suspected bots at the edge without touching origin). Instagram uses edge compute for image resizing — instead of storing 10 pre-rendered sizes of every photo on origin, store one master and resize on-demand at the edge. The trade-off is that edge functions have strict CPU and memory limits (Cloudflare Workers: 50 ms CPU, 128 MB RAM) and cannot easily maintain state across requests — they are request transformers, not full applications.

Real-world examples ground all of this. **Netflix Open Connect** is Netflix's purpose-built CDN: rather than renting capacity from Akamai, Netflix ships free physical appliances (OCAs — Open Connect Appliances) into ISP datacenters worldwide, pre-loaded with Netflix's video catalog. By some estimates Netflix is 15% of global downstream internet traffic, and Open Connect serves ~95% of it from inside the user's ISP — meaning the bytes never traverse the public internet backbone. **Akamai** delivers ~30% of internet traffic, ~200 Tbps peak, with 4,000+ locations in 134 countries. **Instagram** uses CloudFront for static assets (JS, CSS, images) — a user in Tokyo fetches the JS bundle from a Tokyo CloudFront PoP in 5 ms instead of from a US-East origin in 200 ms. **YouTube** uses Google's own edge network (GFE — Google Front End) to cache video chunks close to users, with adaptive bitrate streaming over HTTP. **Amazon CloudFront** is integrated with S3 (origin pull is essentially free because S3 is the origin) and with Lambda@Edge for edge transforms.

The trade-offs of CDNs are real. (1) **Cost** — CDNs charge per GB delivered, and at high traffic volumes (petabytes/month) the bill can be significant; many companies negotiate committed-use discounts. (2) **Cache consistency** — purging across thousands of PoPs takes time (seconds to minutes), so users in different regions may see different versions of the same content for a brief window. (3) **Origin thundering herd** — a cache miss on a hot URL, or a global purge, can spike origin traffic 100x in seconds. (4) **Dynamic content** — CDNs are great for static content but provide less benefit for dynamic, per-user content; you have to use edge compute or per-user cache keys to extract value. (5) **Debugging** — when a CDN serves the wrong content, debugging is hard because the issue is at the edge, not the origin; you need to know which PoP served the request and what it had cached. CDNs connect to other system design concepts as the natural extension of caching (Phase 4), latency reduction (Phase 1 Topic 8), DNS-based geographic routing (Phase 2 Topic 6), and TLS termination (Phase 2 Topic 5). They are also the foundation of edge computing and increasingly of serverless architectures.

### ASCII Diagram
```
   +-----------+      +-----------+      +-----------+
   | User Tokyo|      |User Berlin|      | User NYC  |
   +-----+-----+      +-----+-----+      +-----+-----+
         |                  |                  |
         v                  v                  v
   +-----------+      +-----------+      +-----------+
   | Tokyo PoP |      |Berlin PoP |      |  NYC PoP  |   <-- edges (cache)
   | cache hit |      | cache hit |      | cache MISS|
   |  -> 5 ms  |      |  -> 4 ms  |      |  -> 80 ms |
   +-----------+      +-----------+      +-----+-----+
                                               |
                                  +------------+-----------+
                                  | origin pull (on miss)  |
                                  v                        |
                          +------------------+             |
                          | Origin (us-east) |<------------+
                          |  S3 / API server |
                          +------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
                          +------------------+
                          | Edge caches obj  |
                          | next request: hit|
                          +------------------+

Models:
  Origin pull (Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront):
    user -> edge -> (miss) -> origin -> cache + return
    user -> edge -> (hit)  -> return from cache

  Origin push (Netflix Open Connect):
    origin pre-positions content into edges during off-peak
    user -> edge -> (hit) -> return from cache
    origin NEVER sees the thundering herd at peak

Cache-Control headers:
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600, stale-while-revalidate=60
  Cache-Tag: product-1234,category-shoes   <-- surrogate keys for purging

Invalidation:
  - TTL expires -> next request re-fetches
  - Soft purge  -> mark stale, serve stale-while-revalidate
  - Instant purge (Fastly ~150ms, Cloudflare ~30s) -> evict immediately
```

### Walkthrough
1. A user in Tokyo requests `https://images.example.com/photo.jpg`. The user's DNS resolver (via Route 53 latency-based routing) returns the IP of the Tokyo edge PoP, so the request travels only ~5 ms to the edge.
2. The Tokyo edge checks its cache for the cache key `images.example.com/photo.jpg`. On a hit, it serves the bytes directly in ~5 ms. On a miss, it forwards the request to the origin (us-east-1 S3), which takes ~150 ms; the edge caches the response with the configured TTL and serves it to the user.
3. Subsequent requests from any Tokyo user hit the cache and return in ~5 ms. When the publisher pushes a new version of `photo.jpg`, they call the CDN's purge API with the surrogate key `product-1234`, which evicts the cached entry across all edges within ~30 seconds. The next request re-fetches from origin with `stale-while-revalidate` to avoid a thundering herd.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Return (body, served_from, latency_ms).
- Evict all objects with the given surrogate key.
- Pick nearest edge to user, fetch through it.
- CDN simulator: N edge caches, one origin, LRU eviction, simulated per-region
- Latency. Demonstrates origin pull, cache hit/miss, and thundering-herd risk.
- Cache miss -> origin pull
- LRU eviction if at capacity
- Simulate origin latency: 100ms base + 5ms per KB

**Defines:** `CachedObject`, `EdgeCache`, `Origin`, `CDN`, `simulate_cdn()`

```python
# CDN simulator: N edge caches, one origin, LRU eviction, simulated per-region
# latency. Demonstrates origin pull, cache hit/miss, and thundering-herd risk.

import time
from collections import OrderedDict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class CachedObject:
    key: str
    body: bytes
    ttl_seconds: int
    cached_at: float
    surrogate_keys: set = field(default_factory=set)

    def fresh(self, now: float) -> bool:
        return now < self.cached_at + self.ttl_seconds

@dataclass
class EdgeCache:
    name: str
    region: str
    latency_to_origin_ms: float
    capacity: int                                  # max objects in cache
    store: "OrderedDict[str, CachedObject]" = field(default_factory=OrderedDict)
    stats: dict = field(default_factory=lambda: {"hits": 0, "misses": 0,
                                                  "origin_fetches": 0,
                                                  "evictions": 0})

    def get(self, key: str, origin: "Origin", now: float) -> tuple:
        """Return (body, served_from, latency_ms)."""
        if key in self.store:
            obj = self.store[key]
            if obj.fresh(now):
                self.store.move_to_end(key)        # LRU touch
                self.stats["hits"] += 1
                return obj.body, "edge-cache", 5.0
            else:
                self.store.pop(key)                # expired

        # Cache miss -> origin pull
        self.stats["misses"] += 1
        self.stats["origin_fetches"] += 1
        body, ttl, surrogate_keys = origin.fetch(key, now)
        # LRU eviction if at capacity
        while len(self.store) >= self.capacity:
            self.store.popitem(last=False)         # evict oldest
            self.stats["evictions"] += 1
        self.store[key] = CachedObject(key, body, ttl, now, surrogate_keys)
        return body, "origin", 5.0 + self.latency_to_origin_ms

    def purge(self, surrogate_key: str) -> int:
        """Evict all objects with the given surrogate key. Returns count."""
        keys_to_evict = [k for k, v in self.store.items()
                         if surrogate_key in v.surrogate_keys]
        for k in keys_to_evict:
            self.store.pop(k)
        return len(keys_to_evict)

@dataclass
class Origin:
    name: str
    catalog: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    fetch_count: int = 0

    def register(self, key: str, body: bytes, ttl: int,
                 surrogate_keys: set) -> None:
        self.catalog[key] = (body, ttl, surrogate_keys)

    def fetch(self, key: str, now: float) -> tuple:
        self.fetch_count += 1
        if key not in self.catalog:
            raise KeyError(f"origin has no object for {key}")
        body, ttl, surrogate_keys = self.catalog[key]
        # Simulate origin latency: 100ms base + 5ms per KB
        time.sleep(0.001)                          # tiny real sleep for demo
        return body, ttl, set(surrogate_keys)

@dataclass
class CDN:
    edges: list
    origin: Origin

    def request(self, user_region: str, key: str) -> tuple:
        """Pick nearest edge to user, fetch through it."""
        edge = min(self.edges,
                   key=lambda e: abs(hash(e.region) - hash(user_region)))
        # In real CDNs, DNS routes the user to the nearest PoP.
        return edge.get(key, self.origin, time.time())

    def purge(self, surrogate_key: str) -> dict:
        return {e.name: e.purge(surrogate_key) for e in self.edges}

    def stats(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "origin_fetches": self.origin.fetch_count,
            "edges": {e.name: e.stats for e in self.edges},
        }

def simulate_cdn():
    print("=== CDN Simulator ===\n")
    origin = Origin(name="origin-us-east")
    # Pre-populate origin with some objects
    for i in range(10):
        origin.register(f"/img/photo-{i}.jpg",
                        body=f"<jpeg-bytes-{i}>".encode(),
                        ttl=60,
                        surrogate_keys={f"album-7", f"photo-{i}"})
    origin.register("/js/app.bundle.js",
                    body=b"<js-bytes>" * 100,
                    ttl=3600,
                    surrogate_keys={"frontend", "v1.2.3"})

    edges = [
        EdgeCache("tokyo-edge",  "tokyo",  latency_to_origin_ms=150.0, capacity=5),
        EdgeCache("berlin-edge", "berlin", latency_to_origin_ms=80.0,  capacity=5),
        EdgeCache("nyc-edge",    "nyc",    latency_to_origin_ms=20.0,  capacity=5),
    ]
    cdn = CDN(edges=edges, origin=origin)

    # Scenario 1: Cold cache. Three users in three regions request photo-0.
    print("Scenario 1: Cold caches, three users request /img/photo-0.jpg")
    for region in ("tokyo", "berlin", "nyc"):
        body, source, lat = cdn.request(region, "/img/photo-0.jpg")
        print(f"  {region:8s} -> served from {source:12s}  "
              f"latency={lat:5.1f}ms  body_len={len(body)}B")

    # Scenario 2: Warm cache. Tokyo user re-requests photo-0 (and others).
    print("\nScenario 2: Tokyo user requests 5 photos repeatedly (warm hits)")
    for i in range(5):
        body, source, lat = cdn.request("tokyo", f"/img/photo-{i}.jpg")
        print(f"  request /img/photo-{i}.jpg -> {source:12s}  "
              f"latency={lat:5.1f}ms")

    # Scenario 3: LRU eviction. Tokyo edge has capacity 5, requests 6 distinct
    # objects -> oldest gets evicted, re-request will hit origin.
    print("\nScenario 3: Tokyo edge at capacity 5, request photo-5 (evicts oldest)")
    body, source, lat = cdn.request("tokyo", "/img/photo-5.jpg")
    print(f"  /img/photo-5.jpg -> {source:12s}  latency={lat:5.1f}ms")
    body, source, lat = cdn.request("tokyo", "/img/photo-0.jpg")  # evicted
    print(f"  /img/photo-0.jpg -> {source:12s}  latency={lat:5.1f}ms "
          f"(was evicted, now origin pull again)")

    # Scenario 4: Surrogate-key purge across all edges
    print("\nScenario 4: Publish new album-7, purge surrogate key 'album-7' globally")
    print(f"  before purge: tokyo has {len(edges[0].store)} objects cached")
    purged = cdn.purge("album-7")
    print(f"  purged counts per edge: {purged}")
    print(f"  after purge:  tokyo has {len(edges[0].store)} objects cached")

    # Scenario 5: Stats
    print("\nScenario 5: Final stats")
    s = cdn.stats()
    print(f"  origin total fetches: {s['origin_fetches']}")
    for name, st in s["edges"].items():
        print(f"  {name}: hits={st['hits']} misses={st['misses']} "
              f"origin_fetches={st['origin_fetches']} evictions={st['evictions']}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    simulate_cdn()
```

quiz.question: What problem does a CDN solve, and when would you NOT use one?
options: The bottleneck is almost certainly the 200 ms RTT between Asian users and the US-East origin, multiplied by the multiple round trips needed for TCP + TLS + HTTP.
Five levers. (1) Increase cache hit ratio — every cache hit is served from the edge (cheap); every miss is an origin fetch (expensive in origin CPU + egress).
Two layers. (1) Surrogate-key purge, not URL purge — assign every article a surrogate key (Cache-Tag: article-12345) and purge by key, which is faster than URL-by-URL purging.
A CDN reduces latency for users geographically far from your origin, offloads bandwidth and TLS handshake cost from your origin, and absorbs traffic spikes by serving…
quiz.explanation: A CDN reduces latency for users geographically far from your origin, offloads bandwidth and TLS handshake cost from your origin, and absorbs traffic spikes by serving from cache. The fundamental mechanism is edge caching: instead of every user fetching bytes from your origin (which may be 200 ms away), users fetch from a nearby edge PoP (5 ms away). Akamai delivers ~30% of internet traffic this way.

quiz.question: Explain origin pull vs origin push. When is each appropriate?
options: The migration sequence. (1) Configure CloudFront as a parallel CDN — set up the same origin, the same cache behavior, the same TLS certs.
Store one master image on origin (S3) and resize on-demand at the CDN edge.
Three patterns. (1) Geolocation at the edge — Cloudflare and CloudFront expose the user's country via the CF-IPCountry / CloudFront-Viewer-Country header.
Origin pull is the default for web CDNs: the edge fetches content from origin on first request, caches it, and serves subsequent requests from cache until TTL expires.
quiz.explanation: Origin pull is the default for web CDNs: the edge fetches content from origin on first request, caches it, and serves subsequent requests from cache until TTL expires. It is lazy — only content users actually request gets cached. This is appropriate for web assets (JS, CSS, images), API responses that are cacheable, and long-tail content where you cannot predict demand.

quiz.question: What is a cache key, and what are common mistakes in designing one?
options: Traditional CDN caching is passive: it can only return what origin returned, possibly transformed by simple rules (URL rewriting, header injection).
Origin pull is the default for web CDNs: the edge fetches content from origin on first request, caches it, and serves subsequent requests from cache until TTL expires.
The thundering herd happens when a hot URL has no cache entry (just expired, just purged, or first-ever request) and thousands of concurrent users hit origin…
The cache key is the unique identifier under which the CDN stores a cached response.
quiz.explanation: The cache key is the unique identifier under which the CDN stores a cached response. The default is {URL path} + {query string}, but production CDNs let you customize it: include/exclude headers, ignore certain query params, normalize case, vary on Accept-Encoding for compression variants.

(1) TTL expiration — the cached object has a max-age and is considered stale after that many seconds; the next request re-fetches from origin.
